questions.q: Why does this lesson insist the validation of RPO/RTO be reported honestly, even if the numbers aren't flattering?
options: Because Azure automatically publishes the results regardless
Because the entire point of running an unannounced test is defeated if results get rounded favorably afterward, and the board will ask directly whether it actually worked
Because dishonest reporting is technically impossible
Because the numbers are always good, so honesty is never actually tested
questions.explain: A board that mandated this project because of a real breach needs the real answer, not a flattering one.

questions.q: What is the correct endpoint for measuring observed RTO, according to this lesson?
options: The moment the failover command was run
The moment the failover command returned success
The moment the application was genuinely reachable again — not when the command ran or returned success
The moment the DR runbook was opened
questions.explain: The command succeeding and the application actually being usable again are different moments — the honest measurement uses the real end point.

questions.q: How is observed RPO actually measured, according to this lesson?
options: By guessing based on how long the failover took
By comparing the last confirmed write on the old primary before the disaster to the most recent write actually present on the new primary immediately after failover
By checking only the TDE encryption status
RPO cannot actually be measured after the fact
questions.explain: This uses real timestamps from the audit log or application data, not an estimate.

questions.q: In this lesson's worked example, what were the observed RTO and RPO, and did they meet the Lesson 11 targets?
options: Observed RTO of 2 hours and RPO of 10 minutes — both missed
Observed RTO of about 17 minutes 40 seconds and RPO of 44 seconds — both genuine passes against the 1-hour RTO and 5-minute RPO targets
Observed RTO and RPO were both exactly zero
The example doesn't report any specific numbers
questions.explain: Both observed measurements comfortably beat their respective targets in this worked example.

questions.q: What is the correct response if a drill's observed RTO or RPO had exceeded its target?
options: Hide the result and report a pass anyway
Round the numbers favorably so the drill looks clean
Document exactly what happened, identify the specific step that took longer than planned, and feed that back into the runbook as a named improvement
Cancel all future drills
questions.explain: A missed target found in a drill, and fixed, is exactly the safe outcome this exercise exists to produce — better than discovering it during a real disaster.
